# Three-field rotation (`three_field_system`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/agriculture.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Agriculture & food (`agriculture`)
- Deps: helped by heavy_plough, horse_collar_harness, legumes_green_manure
- Core idea: Divide the arable land into three parts: one sown in autumn with wheat or rye, one sown in spring with oats, barley, peas or beans, one left fallow and grazed; rotate every year. Compared with the two-field system (half the land fallow) two thirds of the land bear a crop each year, the work and the harvest risk are spread over two seasons, and the spring field gives oats for horses and legumes that restore the soil. It needs enough summer rain for spring crops, so it suits northern Europe better than the dry Mediterranean.
- Pitfalls:
  - Expecting it to work in dry-summer climates such as Tuscany or Greece, where spring-sown crops fail and two-field rotation persisted for good reason
  - Thinking the fallow is idle land: it is ploughed several times to kill weeds and is manured by grazing stock
  - Forgetting that open-field villages rotate in common; one farmer cannot change the system alone
  - Claiming a sudden Carolingian 'invention'; the spread was slow and regional (8th to 13th century)
- History: rome: 1st c. AD – two-field rotation with fallow is the Mediterranean norm (Columella, Pliny); europe: late 8th c. – White dates early documentary evidence from Carolingian lands to 763; the timing of adoption on individual estates is less certain; general in northern Europe only by the 12th–13th c.; china: by 6th c. AD – multi-year rotations of cereals and legumes without fallow described in the Qimin yaoshu
- Read:
  - Lynn White Jr., Medieval Technology and Social Change (1962)
  - Adriaan Verhulst, The Carolingian Economy (2002)
  - Georges Duby, Rural Economy and Country Life in the Medieval West (1968)
